Log Zero — Orientation

Two projects, one lab, and a much steeper learning curve than I expected.

This summer I joined Professor Yu She's MARS Lab at Purdue, working alongside Dr. Sheeraz Athar on two parallel efforts: a tactile-sensing gripper for robotic manipulation, and an underwater sensing platform built around the BlueROV2. I came in expecting to observe. I left every week with more solder burns, CAD revisions, and open engineering problems than I planned for — in the best way.

What follows is a log spanning the full internship.

LOG 01
JUNE 22

Gripper assembly, then straight into the deep end

Week one started on the tactile-sensing gripper project — assembly, electronics integration, wiring, and soldering to get the system ready for data collection. Once that project moved into its data-collection phase, I shifted onto the lab's autonomous surface vessel and underwater sensing platform: pressure and vacuum-testing the battery compartment, integrating electronics, and installing the propulsion system.

The part I didn't expect to enjoy this much: getting to actually think through design and manufacturability decisions, not just execute someone else's spec.

LOG 02
JUNE 26
BlueROV2, post Heavy Conversion Kit build
Tether management & float hardware staged for build

Building the BlueROV2, from standard kit to Heavy Configuration

This week was hands-on assembly, start to finish: the standard BlueROV2 build, then the move into the Heavy Conversion Kit and tether — Aarav helped with the initial assembly before he headed back to Florida later in the summer. Watching the vehicle actually take shape — frame, thrusters, floats, tether — made the whole platform click in a way spec sheets hadn't.

In parallel, I started CAD modeling a set of clamps for the project, my first real design contribution rather than just a build task.

BlueROV2 Assembly Heavy Conversion Kit CAD Design
LOG 03
JULY 2

A shorter week, a national final, and a wiring puzzle

I was out for part of the week competing at the FBLA National Leadership Conference, where I placed 4th in the nation in Word Processing. Back in the lab Wednesday and Thursday, I kept iterating the clamp mechanism CAD and spent most of my time configuring the BlueROV2's remote controller.

Everything came online except the thruster controls — a wiring issue I flagged to dig into the following week. Small, unglamorous, and exactly the kind of problem that teaches you how a robotic system actually fits together.

LOG 04
JULY 25
Full mechanical assembly — Heavy Kit + Payload Skid, complete

Full assembly complete — then a communication link goes dark

Big milestone: I finished the complete BlueROV2 assembly, including the Heavy Configuration Retrofit Kit and Payload Skid. In parallel, I finalized the CAD for the gripper mechanism, refining it to mount cleanly to the ROV's underside while staying compact. I sourced and integrated the remaining parts — charger, switch, grip tape, Loctite for the watertight seal.

Then, mid-integration, the Fathom-X Tether Interface stopped talking to the surface computer.

FXTI COMMUNICATION LINKDIAGNOSTIC IN PROGRESS
LINK INACTIVE

Working theory: Raspberry Pi or an internal connection inside the electronics enclosure. Next step — open it up and check power, Ethernet, and the tether interface directly.

LOG 05
TWO WEEKS AGO

A night pool test, and a problem that looked like the ROV itself was broken

Ryan joined me for a night test of the BlueROV2 in the pool — the FXTI link was back, the vehicle powered up, and then it just wouldn't drive right. Pushing forward on the controller did nothing predictable; the vehicle wouldn't move cleanly forward or backward in either direction. Vertical thrust — up and down — worked exactly as expected.

The build instructions were partly to blame: the diagram only showed which mount each thruster went in, not which rotational direction (CW vs. CCW) that prop needed to face. I'd installed several clockwise and counter-clockwise props swapped relative to their positions, which meant the horizontal thrusters were fighting each other instead of driving the vehicle forward or back.

THRUSTER DIAGNOSTIC — NIGHT POOL TESTFIELD OBSERVATION
FORWARD / REVERSE THRUST: INVERTED

Vertical thrusters unaffected — only the horizontal (CW/CCW) pair was mismatched to its mount position.

Prop Orientation Field Debugging Night Pool Test
LOG 06
LAST WEEK

The fix: you don't have to move the prop, you can just reverse the wire

Rather than physically re-mount the thrusters, I spent the week digging into how the motors actually connect to the control hub. Each thruster's brushless DC motor runs on three leads into the hub. Swap any two of the three and you reverse the motor's rotation — effectively flipping a CW thruster to spin CCW (and vice versa) without touching the prop or housing at all.

That meant I could correct the mismatched thrusters entirely at the wiring level. Phillip, one of the lab's grad students, helped me troubleshoot and confirm the fix before we put it back in the water.

THRUSTER DIAGNOSTIC — POST‑FIXRESOLVED
FORWARD / REVERSE THRUST: NOMINAL
Motor Wiring Polarity Reversal Root-Cause Fix
SPOTLIGHT
CAD DEEP‑DIVE

Modeling the gripper before trusting it in the water

Before committing to a physical build, I modeled the full BlueROV2 assembly in CAD to simulate and visualize how the gripper would mount and integrate with the vehicle — checking clearance around the thrusters and camera dome before cutting any material. Earlier in the summer I co-designed the mechanism with fellow intern Aarav; I've kept refining the model since.

The gripper rotates on a geared ring mechanism, driven by a small pinion gear rather than a direct-drive motor — visible in the close-up below, along with the reference planes I used to keep everything aligned while modeling.

LOG 07
AUGUST
Night pool test — full team in the water
Trim test, six-float configuration
Piloting mid-dive

Back in the water — thrusters fixed, and a successful buoyancy test

With the thruster wiring corrected and the FXTI link stable, the BlueROV2 went back in the pool for a full night of testing — this time driving exactly as it should in every direction. Anne came out to test with me, and the focus was buoyancy tuning: we ran the vehicle with six flotation modules and compared trim, stability, and control response against a four-float configuration.

The test came back successful — a clean read on how flotation count changes the vehicle's neutral buoyancy and handling, which now feeds directly into how we finalize the payload and gripper integration going forward.

THRUSTER + FXTI STATUSRESOLVED
BUOYANCY TEST — PASS
Buoyancy Tuning Underwater Field Test 6 vs. 4 Float Trial

End of Summer — MARS Lab

A lab is really its people first

The MARS Lab team — send-off for Dr. Sheeraz Athar and Professor Luu

Sending off Dr. Sheeraz Athar and Professor Luu

Somewhere between the pool tests and the CAD revisions, the lab took a break to celebrate two people moving on to their next chapters: Dr. Sheeraz Athar, who mentored me through nearly every part of this internship, from that first week of soldering to the FXTI troubleshoot, and Professor Luu. Cake, pizza, and a lab's worth of people who made the last few months what they were.

It's easy to describe a summer like this in terms of hardware — ROVs, grippers, CAD files. The bigger part of it was the people who took the time to teach, correct, and mentor along the way.

Log Entries So Far — Summer Continues

The link came back. The testing didn't stop.

This log runs June through August at the MARS Lab — and it's already taught me more about how mechanical, electrical, and software systems actually come together than any classroom could. The most valuable parts were the failures: a dead link, a wiring bug, a gripper redesign. The FXTI connection came back online, the BlueROV2 passed its buoyancy trial, and the gripper is next in line for underwater trials.
